wittgenstein.label: Ludwig Wittgenstein
wittgenstein.description: Language and meaning are situated in shared practices and forms of life. Geertz draws on this account of public meaning in interpreting culture. The Investigations examines varied uses of language, overlapping family resemblances and the practice of following rules. Skinner later explicitly credits its attention to use in developing his historical questions.
wittgenstein.representative_figures_and_works: Philosophical Investigations (1953). This is the later Wittgenstein; it is not a claim that all interpretive anthropology derives from him.
wittgenstein.scope_note: The later philosophy revises earlier assumptions without forming a general historical theory. The meaning/use formulation in §43 is explicitly qualified; agreement in forms of life is not a claim that majority opinion creates truth. The preface acknowledges Ramsey’s conversations and Sraffa’s criticism. Philosophical similarity to Ryle does not establish a single transmission direction.

geertz.label: Clifford Geertz
geertz.description: Culture consists of publicly interpretable meanings. Thick description reconstructs the contexts that make actions intelligible; it is more than adding descriptive detail. “Deep Play” (1972) reads cockfighting through status and symbolic action; Negara (1980) examines ritual and political authority in nineteenth-century Bali. These are his interpretations, with their empirical reach open to debate.
geertz.representative_figures_and_works: The Interpretation of Cultures (1973). Weber, Wittgenstein, and Ryle are explicit interlocutors; the approach becomes influential in cultural history.
geertz.scope_note: Thick description interprets public, situated meanings and constrains interpretations through evidence. Hunt’s adaptation is a specific historical reception; Asad’s religion-category criticism targets a particular argument. These readings do not summarize every Indonesian or Moroccan study or establish a uniform Geertzian cultural history.

levistrauss.label: Claude Lévi-Strauss
levistrauss.description: Analyzes kinship and myth through underlying relations, oppositions, and transformations. Structural explanation differs from Geertz’s interpretation of situated public meanings. The Savage Mind (1962; English 1966) uses bricolage to examine recombination of available signs and materials, while rejecting an evolutionary ranking of mythical and scientific thought.
levistrauss.representative_figures_and_works: The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949); Structural Anthropology (1958). Engagements with history vary; structuralism is not simply any interest in social structures.
levistrauss.scope_note: Relational models are distinct from simply studying social structure. The historical and linguistic chapters connect evidence and formal explanation without identifying anthropology with history. English 1963 passages are from the revised 1958 collection. Later adaptations by Hall and Hebdige, and Derrida’s criticism, are separately evidenced; the Braudel and Lacan exchanges still need stronger passage checks.

barthes.label: Roland Barthes
barthes.date_label: Semiology → textual plurality · Mythologies 1957 · author essay 1967
barthes.description: Analyzes myth as the naturalization of historically produced meanings and studies how historical narratives signify reality. His challenge to authorial closure shifts attention to textual plurality and the reader. Historians and cultural theorists adapt these arguments while disputing their scope.
barthes.representative_figures_and_works: Mythologies (1957); “The Death of the Author” (1967); S/Z (1970).
barthes.scope_note: Individual thinker with a changing trajectory, not one fixed structuralist method. Mythologies (1957), Elements of Semiology (1964), the history/authorship essays (1967), The Reality Effect (1968) and S/Z (1970) are distinct works. Saussure, Jakobson, Kristeva, Nietzsche, Marx and Vernant are named resources with different scopes. Bann questions the implied decline of historians’ concern with reality; Hebdige makes a particular style-analysis adaptation. Rhetorical effects do not alone establish that events are imaginary, and the theoretical reader is not a biography of actual readers. S/Z and later photographic inquiry await bounded primary reading; the clinical analogies and sweeping historical generalizations remain attributed.

lacan.label: Jacques Lacan
lacan.date_label: Freud reread through language · Rome report 1953 · Écrits 1966
lacan.description: Rereads Freud through identification, language and symbolic relations. The mirror-stage argument explains ego unity through an external image; later work recasts dream condensation and displacement through metaphor and metonymy. His divided subject becomes a resource and a problem for historical accounts of gender.
lacan.representative_figures_and_works: Freud is a fundamental antecedent; Saussure, Jakobson, and Lévi-Strauss inform Lacan’s approach. Écrits (1966).
lacan.scope_note: Individual thinker, not a uniform school. The 1949 mirror-stage paper, 1953 report first published in 1956, 1957 linguistic essay and 1966 Écrits collection are distinct witnesses. Saussure’s diagram is transformed, Jakobson explicitly credited, and Lévi-Strauss named as a resource. Althusser appropriates his reading of Freud; Scott finds constructed subjectivity instructive but questions universal sexual antagonism and limited historical variability. These are situated theoretical arguments, not independently established clinical or developmental facts. Later seminars and revisions remain outside this bounded primary reading.

althusser.label: Louis Althusser
althusser.description: Reinterprets Marx through problematics, an epistemological break and overdetermined contradictions. Political and ideological circumstances have explanatory force; material institutions and practices constitute subjects while remaining sites of class struggle. Collective reading, later qualifications and disputes over evidence and agency shape the program.
althusser.representative_figures_and_works: For Marx and Reading Capital (1965). E. P. Thompson’s The Poverty of Theory (1978) directly attacks his approach.
althusser.scope_note: Individual thinker whose positions change; neither all Marxism nor a timeless structuralist system. For Marx and the five-author Reading Capital appeared in 1965; the consulted revised abridgment omits three contributors and acknowledges a unilateral theoreticism. Bachelard, Martin, Canguilhem, Cavaillès, Foucault, Lacan and Gramsci supply named resources with different evidential scopes. Thompson’s criticism and Hall’s productive disagreement are distinct interventions. Interpellation is a theoretical illustration, not a chronological experiment; apparatuses also involve resistance and struggle beyond institutions. Later political revisions and other collaborators’ original chapters remain bounded research limits.

foucault.label: Michel Foucault
foucault.date_label: The Order of Things 1966 · Discipline and Punish 1975 · Sexuality I 1976
foucault.description: Studies how objects of knowledge and subjects take shape through historically specific practices. Archaeology examines discursive formations; genealogy traces contingent descent and emergence. Power works through actions upon possible actions, with institutions, resistance and changing forms of subjectivity entering the analysis.
foucault.representative_figures_and_works: The Order of Things (1966); Discipline and Punish (1975); History of Sexuality I (1976). His association with structuralism is contested.
foucault.scope_note: Individual thinker with changing projects, not a uniform structuralist school. History of Madness (1961), archaeological inquiry, genealogy and the 1982 account of subjects are distinct contexts. Canguilhem and Nietzsche supply named resources. Derrida’s challenge and Foucault’s reply concern reason, madness, Descartes and discursive practice; neither settles their whole relationship. Historians including Scott, Chartier, Goldstein, Said and Stoler adapt and criticize different aspects, with separately scoped evidence. Comparative historical generalizations remain attributed. Later ethics and self-practice require further bounded primary reading.

derrida.label: Jacques Derrida
derrida.description: Works through conceptual hierarchies and the conditions of signification, writing and historical transmission. Critical engagements with Saussure, Husserl, Heidegger and Foucault distinguish deconstruction from a single structuralist method. His archive inquiry connects institutions, access, inscription and preservation with psychoanalytic questions.
derrida.representative_figures_and_works: “Structure, Sign, and Play” (1966); Of Grammatology (1967). Husserl and Heidegger are further important interlocutors beyond the links selected here.
derrida.scope_note: Individual thinker whose arguments change across works. Of Grammatology (French 1967; first American 1976; corrected English 1997) is distinct from the 1963 Cogito lecture, 1983 Japanese letter and 1994 archive lecture. Peirce, Freud and historian Sonia Combe are explicit resources in the selected passages. Scott and Spivak offer particular productive uses; Foucault supplies a specific objection. Deconstruction is not a license for arbitrary readings or a claim that institutions reduce to books. The original French witnesses, full archive argument and Austin/Searle exchange remain outside this bounded primary reading.

economic.label: Economic history
economic.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms
economic.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
economic.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988). Richard White, Railroaded (2011): corporate finance, public subsidies and political markets; selected author interview passages checked.

strands.title: Historical economics and disciplinary institutions
strands.focus: Historical specificity and institutional research; formation of a field does not establish one doctrine.
strands.works: Schmoller’s methodological review (1883); Cunningham’s textbook (1882); Ashley and disciplinary institutions

strands.focus: Economic life studied through social relations, belief, households, and women’s work.
strands.works: Tawney, Religion and the Rise of Capitalism; Power, Medieval People; Clark and Pinchbeck on women’s labour

strands.title: French serial and conjunctural history
strands.focus: Simiand and Labrousse investigate different economic movements. Later rereadings distinguish construction of evidence, causal conditions and routine series; uneven crises need not fit one automatic sequence.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956); Grenier/Lepetit (1989); Simonin (1992)

strands.title: Capitalist development and contested production relations
strands.focus: Coercion, markets, wage labour and the state are related explanatory problems. Dobb’s reply acknowledges uncertainty about one accumulation hypothesis; Sweezy and Takahashi pose different challenges.
strands.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167; Takahashi (1952); Unwin (1904)

strands.title: Cliometrics and historical measurement
strands.focus: Economic models and quantitative evidence; neither all economic history nor all quantitative history.
strands.works: Fogel, “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology” (1993); North, “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Institutions and economic change
strands.focus: Rules, incentives, learning, and historical paths; overlaps with cliometrics without being identical to it.
strands.works: North, Economic Performance through Time

strands.title: Slavery, empire, and unequal development
strands.focus: Different arguments about capitalist development and colonial power; Drescher contests the decline explanation for British slave-trade abolition.
strands.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); Econocide (1977)

strands.title: Market society and nonmarket economic relations
strands.focus: Polanyi distinguishes a market-regulated economy from reciprocity and redistribution; his broad historical claims are arguments to examine, not settled descriptions of every society.
strands.works: The Great Transformation (1944), chapter IV

strands.title: Different paths of later industrialization
strands.focus: Compare technology borrowing, industrial scale and the roles of banks and states; later industrializers need not repeat England’s sequence.
strands.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection)

strands.title: Household labor, demand and industrious change
strands.focus: Changes in household resource allocation can increase market labor and demand together. Household members’ interests differ, and the proposed pattern is not universal.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.
strands.works: The Great Divergence (2000)

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.
strands.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977)

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.
strands.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability
strands.focus: Tawney distinguishes regional and temporal patterns, tenant and landlord activity, legal forms and economic pressures. His introduction treats incomplete statistics and incompatible records as problems of inference.
strands.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.
strands.works: Furtado (1959/2005), XXXI–XXXII opening; Novais (1961)

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.
strands.works: Fogel/Engerman (1977), opening; David/Temin (1979),213–214

strands.title: Household production and disputed divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s 2002 review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.
strands.works: Pomeranz (2000),17; Huang and Pomeranz (2002), selected retrospective passages; Huang’s rejoinder and Pomeranz’s response (2003)

strands.title: Coal, constraints and competing explanations
strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

strands.title: Wealth and the measurement of goods
strands.focus: Weatherill acknowledges Shammas’s challenge: ownership patterns associated with occupation or towns may reflect wealth. Their different data constructions ask different questions.
strands.works: Weatherill (1996),xviii–xix and notes17,20

strands.title: Agrarian labour and recorded categories
strands.focus: Kumar’s southern Indian inquiry combines documentary interpretation with quantitative reconstruction. Her stated caste/occupation assumptions must remain visible when discussing estimates.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

strands.title: Population and the character of industrial growth
strands.focus: Wrigley investigates population change and the contingent character of industrial growth. This bounded summary follows the Economic History Society account and the publisher excerpts of Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8) and Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11); People, Cities and Wealth (1987) is unread.
strands.works: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988)

economic.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

memory.description: Studies remembering, commemoration and forgetting through social relations, narratives, bodies and cultural forms. Recollection is evidence requiring interpretation; memory and history are connected in different, contested ways.

memory.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering
strands.focus: Family, religious and class contexts organize recollection; a collective framework is not proof of one identical group memory.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); English selections (1992)

strands.title: Sites of memory and historical reconstruction
strands.focus: Sites combine material, symbolic and functional dimensions, extending beyond monuments alone.
strands.works: “Between Memory and History” (1989)

strands.title: Habit, bodies and ceremony
strands.focus: Remembering includes bodily competence, not only recalled propositions or pictures.
strands.works: How Societies Remember (1989), “Bodily practices”

strands.title: Communication and cultural objectivation
strands.focus: Everyday recollection and durable cultural forms operate differently; Assmann revises rather than merely repeats Halbwachs.
strands.works: Jan Assmann (1988/1995); Aleida Assmann (1999)

strands.title: Media and uses of cultural memory
strands.focus: Writing, images and monuments organize what can be stored and recalled.
strands.works: Erinnerungsräume (1999)

strands.title: Mourning and cultural continuities after war
strands.focus: Traditional and modern forms overlap in Great War mourning; this is not a template for every subsequent catastrophe.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

strands.title: Holocaust memorials and their contexts
strands.focus: Memorial forms and meanings vary across places and institutions.
strands.works: The Texture of Memory (1993)

strands.title: Popular practices of historical knowledge
strands.focus: Family research, images and reenactment make historical work visible outside professional writing.
strands.works: Theatres of Memory (1994)

strands.title: Life histories, gender and subjectivity
strands.focus: Fascist everyday life and feminist psychoanalytic inquiry are distinct routes into interpreted recollection.
strands.works: Passerini (1987); Alexander (1994)

strands.title: Archival authority, access and inscription
strands.focus: Combe’s inquiry into access supplies a named resource to Derrida. His account differentiates archives from spontaneous memory and examines institutional authority and technical inscription. From the archival profession, Schwartz and Cook called archives 'active sites where social power is negotiated' whose appraisal and access shape collective memory (2002, abstract); the wider readership is on the entry archival_turn.
strands.works: Archives interdites (1994); Archive Fever (1994/1996)

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public memory
strands.focus: Hayden’s collaborative practice links historical interpretation to lived places.
strands.works: The Power of Place (1995)

strands.title: Traditions in contact and conflict
strands.focus: Halbwachs explains revisions of collective remembering through contact with other groups and their traditions; social frameworks are not an assurance of a unanimous or unchanging past.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925), final concluding subsection

strands.title: Memorial production and public disagreement
strands.focus: Young’s Saarbrücken account follows a covert art project into public controversy and political recognition. His interpretation makes the memorial’s production and reception part of its meaning.
strands.works: Germany’s vanishing Holocaust monuments (1994), adapted extract

strands.title: Argentina: rights, remembrance and generations
strands.focus: Jelin examines competing public memories and tensions within human-rights activism. Her conclusion questions both political forgetting and repetition that prevents younger generations from reinterpreting the past.
strands.works: The Politics of Memory (1994), selected sections

strands.title: Vichy’s afterlife and historical inquiry
strands.focus: Rousso distinguishes memory as an object of research, as a preliminary examination of inherited representations, and as a way to extend an event’s historical study into its aftermath.
strands.works: Pour une histoire de la mémoire collective (1991), 163–166

strands.title: Jewish remembrance and historiography
strands.focus: Yerushalmi’s prologue asks why concern with historical meaning and remembrance need not give professional historical writing the central role. This is a situated historical question, not a timeless definition of Jewish people.
strands.works: Zakhor (1982), selected prologue passages

fanon.label: Frantz Fanon
fanon.description: Analyzes colonial domination through racialized experience, psychic injury, and struggles for liberation. A psychiatrist and political theorist whose work supplies historians with questions about subject formation, violence, and the limits of national liberation; his arguments are not confined to individual psychology.
fanon.representative_figures_and_works: Black Skin, White Masks (French original 1952); The Wretched of the Earth (French original 1961). Later English editions have different publication dates.
fanon.scope_note: Black Skin, White Masks (1952) treats racialized experience through psychological and social explanation; its introduction names Freud while insisting on sociogeny. The Wretched of the Earth (1961) combines liberation strategy, criticism of elite nationalism and psychiatric cases. These are connected inquiries, not one invariant doctrine or membership in psychohistory. Gendered and regional generalizations require critical reading.

rodney.label: Walter Rodney
rodney.description: Explains underdevelopment through historically unequal relations of slavery, colonial extraction and capitalism. Regional African research, Guyanese labor history and popular education give his work distinct scales and audiences. His account of systemic constraints also investigates changing societies; dependency analysis captures only part of his scholarship and politics.
rodney.representative_figures_and_works: The Groundings with My Brothers (1969); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972).
rodney.scope_note: A History of the Upper Guinea Coast, 1545–1800 (1970, from a 1966 thesis) reconstructs regional change; The Groundings with My Brothers (1969) concerns political education; How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) offers a didactic synthesis. A History of the Guyanese Working People, 1881–1905 (posthumous, 1981) examines labor and racial divisions. His 1975 Marxism lecture distinguishes method from fixed European conclusions. James’s later strategic criticism coexists with formative intellectual exchange.

Collaborative projects and Duerr’s criticism qualify the range of this inquiry; book bodies and reception are checked separately.

frances_yates.label: Frances A. Yates
frances_yates.date_label: Renaissance culture and arts of memory · 1960s–70s
frances_yates.description: Investigates mnemonic techniques, images and Renaissance intellectual culture through textual and visual reconstruction. The Art of Memory distinguishes traditions of remembering and argues that their transformations matter to the history of knowledge. Named collaborators and critics help expose both the resources and risks of this inquiry.
frances_yates.representative_figures_and_works: The Art of Memory (1966), including its treatment of Renaissance memory systems and questions about scientific method. Her historical interpretations are arguments for assessment, not a single uncontested model of Renaissance thought.
frances_yates.scope_note: The complete preface and concluding chapter distinguish classical rhetoric, medieval prudence, Lullism and Renaissance occult memory. Yates uses Rossi without claiming identical approaches; Bing mediates Warburg’s image questions, and Walker and R. W. Yates contribute specific work. Leibniz and secret-transmission arguments retain their hypothetical or contested status. Mnemonic arts differ from collective commemoration; Yates is not assigned a Skinner-derived method or Cambridge School membership.

ep_thompson.label: E. P. Thompson
ep_thompson.description: Makes culture, experience, and agency central to the historical formation of class, contributing to an early cultural reorientation within Marxist social history. He retained materialist explanation while disputing other uses of culture and theory. Feminist historians developed resources from his work while criticizing its handling of gender; he resisted some of their extensions and criticisms. This is an intertwined history of inheritance and disagreement, not a simple replacement of class by culture.

eric_hobsbawm.label: Eric Hobsbawm
eric_hobsbawm.date_label: Primitive Rebels 1959 · The Age of… 1962–1994 · The Invention of Tradition 1983 · Budapest lecture 1993 · Interesting Times 2002 · How to Change the World 2011 · Fractured Times 2013
eric_hobsbawm.description: A historian of labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and nations, who studies cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis across different scales; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others. After Primitive Rebels (1959) and Labouring Men (1964), his four Age of… volumes (1962–1994) became, for reviewers, a synthesis of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991; Tony Judt called The Age of Capital his greatest work and criticised The Age of Extremes for keeping the political categories of the 1930s (1995). With Terence Ranger he edited The Invention of Tradition (1983); in a 1993 lecture in Budapest he told historians to resist national myths as they formed and to hold to the difference between fact and fiction. Later books include On History (1997); the memoir Interesting Times (2002), which Perry Anderson read as a fifth volume of the same project: he finds in its explanation of remaining Communist after 1956 what most readers would see as integrity, while faulting its limited engagement with the political history of European Communism and its treatment of other Marxists; How to Change the World (2011), a history of Marxism, which Terry Eagleton credits with judiciousness while criticising its handling of ideas, including Althusser, feminism and Trotskyism; and the posthumous Fractured Times (2013).
eric_hobsbawm.representative_figures_and_works: Primitive Rebels (1959); The Age of Revolution (1962); Labouring Men (1964); Industry and Empire (1968); Bandits (1969; revised 2000); The Age of Capital (1975); response to Stone on narrative (1980); with Terence Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); The Age of Empire (1987); Nations and Nationalism since 1780 (1990); “The New Threat to History” (1993); The Age of Extremes (1994); On History (1997); Interesting Times (2002); Globalisation, Democracy and Terrorism (2007); How to Change the World (2011); Fractured Times (2013). Readings: Judt (1995); Anderson (2002); Black (2003–4); Eagleton (2011); Morgan (2013); Mayer on Evans’s biography (2020).
eric_hobsbawm.scope_note: The 1980 narrative reply, Bandits in its revised 2000 form, and Nations and Nationalism (1990/1992) distinguish debate, self-revision and historical synthesis. Later concessions about myth and political power are not projected into 1969. Colombian interlocutors and European comparative models supply named resources. Labouring Men and the main nationalism cases remain unread; selected primary support does not audit his entire career or generalizations. The 1993 Budapest lecture is read in full. The Age of… volumes, Primitive Rebels, Industry and Empire, On History, Interesting Times, How to Change the World and Fractured Times are unread here; they are dated and characterised through named readers (Judt, Anderson, Black, Eagleton, Morgan, the Guardian obituarists, and Mayer on Evans’s 2019 biography). No reception of The Invention of Tradition or of Nations and Nationalism is read here: the 1983 volume rests on its publisher record and the 1990 book on its preview, and Judt’s review and the 1993 lecture do not supply that reception. Criticism of individual contributors to the 1983 volume is not criticism of Hobsbawm’s conceptual programme.

roger_chartier.label: Roger Chartier
roger_chartier.date_label: Lectures et lecteurs 1987 · Le monde comme représentation 1989 · Les origines culturelles 1990 · questions to White 1993 · “La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ?” 2003 · Collège de France 2007–2016 · Cardenio 2011 · Éditer et traduire 2021
roger_chartier.description: A historian of reading, the book and written culture in early modern Europe who explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme, set out in “Le monde comme représentation” (1989), joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation. In 1993 he put four questions to Hayden White, on language, tropology, the procedures of research and relativism before the Shoah; they are known here through White’s 1995 rejoinder. In 2003 he argued that practices cannot be reduced to discourse, doubted that the new cultural history was as coherent as Lynn Hunt had claimed, and described it as a space of debate that had moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn”. He held the Collège de France chair “Écrit et cultures dans l’Europe moderne” from 2007 to 2016; his inaugural lecture called the tide of digital textuality a major rupture in the history of written culture, as his reviewer Christian Jouhaud quotes it. Later books, known here through their reviewers, follow the mobility of texts: the lost play Cardenio between Cervantes and Shakespeare (2011) and Éditer et traduire (2021).

Readings: White (1995); Jouhaud (2008, 2022); Boucheron (2014).
roger_chartier.scope_note: The 1989 article explicitly engages McKenzie, Ricœur, Fish, Marin, Durkheim/Mauss, Elias, Ginzburg, Certeau and Foucault. Productive Foucault use coexists with a different account of appropriation; criticism of Braudel concerns an explanatory hierarchy. Social divisions include gender, generation, religion and education as well as class. natalie_zemon_davis.date_label: “The Reasons of Misrule” 1971 · “The Rites of Violence” 1973 · Society and Culture in Early Modern France 1975 · “Women’s History in Transition” 1976 · The Return of Martin Guerre 1982–83 · Fiction in the Archives 1987 · Women on the Margins 1995 · Slaves on Screen and The Gift 2000 · Trickster Travels 2006
natalie_zemon_davis.description: A historian of sixteenth-century France whose work moved from the social history of Lyon’s printing workers to ritual, gender, storytelling and lives that crossed religious and colonial borders. By her own account (1997) she ‘combined archival work with the study of printed texts of multiple genres’, and Laurie Nussdorfer’s memorial calls her ‘the rare social historian who valued printed sources’. In ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973) she argued that religious riot drew on ‘a store of punitive or purificatory traditions’ and had ‘a connection in time, place and form with the life of worship’, so that such violence was ‘related here less to the pathological than to the normal’; she explicitly distinguished explaining the ritual structure of violence from granting a right to commit it: ‘the rites of violence are not the rights of violence in any absolute sense’. She acknowledged the crowd histories of Rudé, Hobsbawm, Thompson and Tilly and applied Thompson’s account of the food riot’s legitimation to the religious crowd. By her own account she came to ritual through Van Gennep’s folklore and read Evans-Pritchard, Turner, Geertz and Mintz ‘eclectically … not looking for solutions, but for questions’ (1997); Thompson, for his part, called her charivari essay ‘une étude importante’ (1972). Joan Scott (1986) quoted her call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ as an early relational use of gender, and with Jill Conway she taught in 1971 what she called ‘the first course in women’s history in Canada’. In 1997 she said she came to microhistory, ‘or what I called ethnography’, through the film of Martin Guerre, on whose script she worked; her book followed in French (1982) and English (1983). Robert Finlay (1988) charged that she had ‘permitted an excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’; she answered that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question I hoped readers would ask’. In her 1997 retrospect she described the ‘fiction’ of Fiction in the Archives (1987) as ‘the crafting element’, not falsification, and Women on the Margins (1995) as ‘a decentered comparison’ of three lives, whose conclusion keeps religious difference and colonial domination in view. The Holberg committee (2010) described The Gift (2000) as illuminating ‘the intricate forms of pre-market exchange and reciprocity’, Slaves on Screen (2000) as dealing with ‘the alteration of historical material in contemporary film’ and Trickster Travels (2006), with Women on the Margins, as exploring ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’; it saw her uniqueness in ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history’.
natalie_zemon_davis.representative_figures_and_works: Natalie Zemon Davis (1928–2023); dissertation on Lyon’s Protestants and printing workers (1959); “A Trade Union in Sixteenth-Century France” (Economic History Review, 1966); “The Reasons of Misrule: Youth Groups and Charivaris in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1971); “The Rites of Violence: Religious Riot in Sixteenth-Century France” (Past and Present, 1973; reprinted in Society and Culture in Early Modern France, 1975); “‘Women’s History’ in Transition: The European Case” (Feminist Studies, 1976; quoted by Scott, 1986); Le Retour de Martin Guerre (Paris: Robert Laffont, 1982; the catalogue record also credits Jean-Claude Carrière and Daniel Vigne, scenarist and director of the 1982 film on whose script she worked) and The Return of Martin Guerre (Harvard, 1983); “History’s Two Bodies” (AHA presidential address, 1987; AHR 1988); Fiction in the Archives: Pardon Tales and Their Tellers in Sixteenth-Century France (1987); “On the Lame” (AHR Forum, 1988, reply to Finlay); Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995); A Life of Learning (Haskins Lecture, 1997); Slaves on Screen: Film and Historical Vision (2000); The Gift in Sixteenth-Century France (2000); Trickster Travels: A Sixteenth-Century Muslim between Worlds (2006); “Decentering History” (Holberg Symposium, 2010); later titles named in Nussdorfer’s memorial (unread): Leo Africanus Discovers Comedy: Theatre and Poetry Across the Mediterranean (2021) and Listening to the Languages of the People: Lazare Sainéan on Romanian, Yiddish and French (2022). Readers and critics: E. P. Thompson (1972); Lawrence Stone (1979); Joan Scott (1986); Robert Finlay (1988); Lynn Hunt, ed., with Suzanne Desan’s chapter (1989); Judith Jackson Fossett (2001); Holberg Prize committee (2010); Alexandra Walsham (2017); Laurie Nussdorfer (2023); Carla Hesse (2024).
natalie_zemon_davis.scope_note: Read for revision 1.143: ‘The Rites of Violence’ (1973), pp. 52–53, 57, 60–61 and 90–91; her Haskins Lecture, A Life of Learning (1997), in full, cited as her later account of her course, not as evidence of what the earlier works say; ‘On the Lame’ (1988), pp. 572, 574–576, 584, 587, 600 and 602–603; Finlay’s critique (1988) in full; Stone (1979), pp. 3 and 18; Scott (1986), p. 1054; and, earlier, the prologue, conclusion and acknowledgments of Women on the Margins. Thompson’s ‘Rough Music’ (1972, by paragraph in a 2020 reprint), her AHA address (1987) and the AHA memorial (2024) are read only in short excerpts. The Return of Martin Guerre, Fiction in the Archives, The Gift, Slaves on Screen, Trickster Travels and the 2021–22 books are unread: they supply bibliographic dates and mediated interpretations only, given in her own retrospect or in named readers’ words (the Holberg committee, Fossett, Finlay, Nussdorfer). Also unread: ‘Women’s History in Transition’ (1976; her words as Scott quotes them), Estèbe’s 1975 comment on ‘Rites’ and her rejoinder, Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian Martin Guerre, Desan’s 1989 chapter and the Davis–Thompson letters (Walsham 2017; opening only). She is not presented as the founder of microhistory, cultural history or gender history: by her own account Le Roy Ladurie and Ginzburg reached microhistory by other routes, Scott quotes her as one relational voice among others, and anthropology supplied questions tested on ‘only historical evidence’. Finlay’s charge of invention and her reply are both kept, as is Fossett’s criticism (2001) that Slaves on Screen ‘raises more questions than it answers’. Not to be confused with J. C. Davis (the Ranter debate) or Donald F. Davis (Canadian urban history).

catherine_hall.label: Catherine Hall
catherine_hall.date_label: Family Fortunes 1987 · White, Male and Middle Class 1992 · Defining the Victorian Nation 2000 · Civilising Subjects 2002 · Legacies of British Slave-ownership 2009– · Macaulay and Son 2012 · Lucky Valley 2024
catherine_hall.description: A historian of gender, class, race and empire. With Leonore Davidoff she related English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes (1987), investigating class identities and gender relations together rather than in separate accounts. Civilising Subjects (2002), whose “central argument”, she wrote, “is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness”, followed Birmingham abolitionists and Baptist missionaries to Jamaica; she credited C. L. R. James with showing what can be gained by studying “metropole and colony in one lens”. Angela Woollacott (2006) reads it as postcolonial history for its “insistence on the interconstitutive connections between colony and metropole”, and Edward Said (2003) praised it while asking for subaltern voices. From 2009 she led, with her research associates Nicholas Draper and Keith McClelland, University College London’s Legacies of British Slave-ownership project, tracing the slave-owners compensated at emancipation into Victorian Britain. In 2014 she and her coauthors identified a move toward modified versions of Williams’s thesis among economic historians, and she argued, against the British Marxist historians’ neglect of “race, slavery and the Caribbean”, that gender and race shaped the formation of capital. Lucky Valley (2024) turns to Edward Long and “racial capitalism”.
catherine_hall.representative_figures_and_works: With Leonore Davidoff, Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987); White, Male and Middle Class (1992); with Keith McClelland and Jane Rendall, Defining the Victorian Nation (2000); Civilising Subjects: Metropole and Colony in the English Imagination, 1830–1867 (2002); Macaulay and Son: Architects of Imperial Britain (2012); with Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland, Katie Donington and Rachel Lang, Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014); “Gendering Property, Racing Capital” (History Workshop Journal, 2014); Lucky Valley: Edward Long and the History of Racial Capitalism (2024). Joint works; retain all coauthor credits. Readings: Said (2003); Gikandi, Levine and Holt (JBS, 2003, as Hall answers them); Woollacott (2006); Tao Wei (2014).
catherine_hall.scope_note: Equal coauthor credit with Davidoff for Family Fortunes, whose newly checked evidence is the indexed prologue abstract and publisher description of a later edition. Family Fortunes and her imperial and slavery work (2002–2014) are distinct projects linked by attention to gender, class and race. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership is collective work and its edges credit the team. Her 2014 History Workshop Journal essay is read in her own words; Civilising Subjects is presented through her own 2003 reply to its commentators (pp. 530–537, read by a second research pass), Said’s and Woollacott’s readings and its publisher description; the commentators’ own texts are unread; Legacies is read through its jointly written introduction in excerpts without print pages and UCL’s 2014 impact case study; Macaulay and Son through Tao Wei’s review; White, Male and Middle Class, Defining the Victorian Nation and Lucky Valley through contents or publisher descriptions only. She is not Stuart Hall.

cdn_women_gender.label: Canadian women's & gender history
cdn_women_gender.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_women_gender.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.
cdn_women_gender.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier women writers of history: Machar, Skinner, Skelton, Esther Clark Wright, Neatby, Ormsby, Daveluy, as recovered in Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Cleverdon, The Woman Suffrage Movement in Canada (1950). Cook and Mitchinson, eds., The Proper Sphere (1976); Strong-Boag, The Parliament of Women (1976); Kealey, ed., A Not Unreasonable Claim (1979). Collectif Clio, L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982; Quebec Women, 1987); Prentice et al., Canadian Women: A History (1988). Pierson, "They're Still Women After All" (1986); Danylewycz, Taking the Veil (1987); Strong-Boag, The New Day Recalled (1988); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la crise (1991); Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies (1991); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Dubinsky, Improper Advances (1993). Debate: Pierson (1991); Parr (1995); Sangster (1995, 1996); Iacovetta and Kealey (1996); Dubinsky and Marks (1996); Lévesque (1997); Sangster's retrospect (2011). Morgan, Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996); McPherson, Morgan and Forestell, eds., Gendered Pasts (1999); Parr, Domestic Goods (1999); Korinek, Roughing It in the Suburbs (2000); Christie, Engendering the State (2000). Comparison: Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" (1980); Perry, On the Edge of Empire (2001). Later readings: Fahrni (2005), Campbell (2009), Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018), Bienvenue and Dorais, eds., Profession historienne? (2023).
cdn_women_gender.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in Quebec historiography; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to Quebec historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with Moral regulation; childhood and family with Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in Canadian working-class history, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history

Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. settler_colonialism.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999, 2006 · journal 2011 · Tuck and Yang 2012 · critiques 2013–14 · TRC 2015 · Wolfe d. 2016 · Englert 2020 · reviewed through 2024
settler_colonialism.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, took land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe gave the field its programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'invasion is a structure not an event' (1999, 2006). Lorenzo Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011) and distinguished colonialism ('you, work for me') from settler colonialism ('you, go away'), adding that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': it 'extinguishes itself'. Two questions organise this selection: how elimination persists while pursuing its own completion, and how settler-colonial analysis relates to Indigenous sovereignty, refusal and resurgence. Veracini develops Wolfe's formula: self-supersession means the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, not a successful decolonisation. The Indigenous reading adopts Wolfe's formula while insisting that 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies' (Kauanui), that 'decolonization is not a metaphor' (Tuck and Yang) and that refusal, not recognition, answers the settler state (Simpson, Coulthard). Settler scholars warn against 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch); Marxists ask whether elimination or exploitation defines the form (Englert). In Canada the frame met an older historiography of reserves, treaties, gender and the state, and the TRC's finding of 'cultural genocide' (2015).
settler_colonialism.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Sayegh (1965), Rodinson (1973), Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Simpson (2014, 2017), Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014), Moreton-Robinson (2015), Kauanui (2016), Goeman (2016). settler_colonialism.scope_note: A research field whose consolidation came after 2000; reviewed through 2024 in the period-4 wave (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md). Read in full: Wolfe 2006 (in an Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page), Veracini 2011 and his 2016 obituary of Wolfe, Kauanui 2016, Englert 2020, Goeman 2016; in most pages, Tuck and Yang 2012 and Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014; Macoun and Strakosch 2013 in the authors' version; Veracini 2013 in its author manuscript (abstract, opening, conclusion); the TRC summary pp. 1–3. Unread, known through publisher pages or named readers: Wolfe 1999 beyond pp. 1–2, 2001, 2008, 2016; Veracini 2010, 2015; Coulthard; A. Simpson (book; 2017 abstract read); Byrd; Moreton-Robinson; L. B. Simpson; Rowse; Konishi; Sexton; Garba and Sorentino; King; Daschuk; Miller 2009; Perry 2015; Carter 2016; McCallum; Mawani; Stanger-Ross; Lowman and Barker; Regan. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies; Veracini (2013) and Kauanui (2016) both record uses of the term before Wolfe (Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973, Denoon 1983, Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis 1995). Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris, Miller, Daschuk and McCallum wrote earlier or beside it, and their publisher descriptions do not use the phrase. Critics appear as critics; Kauanui and Goeman defend Wolfe's theory against shallow citation while asking the field to attend to Indigenous studies. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: two or more of the field's authors are cited by 3.2% of Canada + US theses in 2000–09 and 11.0% in 2020–25 (Canada 15.2%, US 6.8%); Wolfe and Veracini are co-cited by 3.0% of theses in 2020–25 and Wolfe with Tuck and Yang, Simpson or Coulthard by 2.3% (the release's category 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' names a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position: Tuck and Yang build on Wolfe, and Kauanui criticises his reception), the only rising two-sided citing after 2000; the Canadian neighbourhood of the founders is the largest and youngest of any field (51 works, median year 2006), its 2020–25 entrants Coulthard, Simpson, Carter, Miller, Daschuk, Kauanui and Greer. The earlier pilot of 2026-10-12 (Canadian strict History PhDs, 2009–26) found 54 citing a work of Wolfe's and 17 the 1999 book (first in 2012), and Daschuk the work most co-cited with Wolfe and Veracini (19 of 58); these figures say more about Canadian history than about him. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Francophone uptake in the corpus remains near zero.

strands.title: Structure, not event: the logic of elimination
strands.focus: Wolfe's programme, now read in his own pages. Settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it 'is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'the primary motive for elimination is not race … but access to territory. Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event'; elimination has a 'positive' aspect (allotment, citizenship, child abduction, assimilation) that persists after the frontier, so that the form is 'relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' names its convergence with genocide without 'hierarchy among victims' (2006). The formula goes back to the 1999 book (p. 2) and the 1994 essay (p. 96, per his note 7). Kauanui: the phrase 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement of his theory'.
strands.works: Patrick Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology: The Politics and Poetics of an Ethnographic Event (London and New York: Cassell, 1999). Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).

strands.title: Veracini: the field, the journal and the self-superseding structure
strands.focus: Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011; open access, volunteer-run, on an ARC grant; to Taylor & Francis in 2013) 'to contribute to the consolidation of a new scholarly field'. Colonialism says 'you, work for me'; settler colonialism says 'you, go away'; the two 'should be understood in their dialectical relation'. Developing Wolfe's formula rather than disputing it, he adds that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': 'settler colonialism, by contrast, extinguishes itself' and is 'least visible in the settler cities'. This self-supersession is the settler project's attempted extinction of the settler–Indigenous relation by the disappearance of Indigenous peoples, not a successful decolonisation, which would instead end 'with an indigenous ultimate permanence'; 'decolonisation is not settler decolonisation', and the politics of recognition 'cannot be considered a genuinely decolonising move' (2011). His history of the concept (2013) finds three earlier careers of the term and a consolidation 'from approximately the mid 1990s', with 'both the Canadian and US historiographies … late in adopting' it. Englert calls him Wolfe's 'self-styled intellectual successor'; Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel find in his history 'Indigenous studies and Indigenous resistance … pretty much erased'.
strands.works: Lorenzo Veracini, "Settler Collective, Founding Violence and Disavowal: The Settler Colonial Situation," Journal of Intercultural Studies 29, no. 4 (2008): 363–379.; Lorenzo Veracini, Settler Colonialism: A Theoretical Overview (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010).; Lorenzo Veracini, "Introducing: Settler Colonial Studies," Settler Colonial Studies 1, no. 1 (2011): 1–12.; Lorenzo Veracini, "'Settler Colonialism': Career of a Concept," Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History 41, no. 2 (2013): 313–333.; Edward Cavanagh and Lorenzo Veracini, eds., The Routledge Handbook of the History of Settler Colonialism (London: Routledge, 2017).

strands.focus: Comparative settler economies (1983) and gender, race, ethnicity and class in settler societies (1995) are earlier comparative scholarship, before the field's theoretical consolidation; Veracini's history of the concept records decolonization-era usage of the term itself. Veracini (2013) reads the 'settler/dominion capitalism' literature as writing 'indigenous people and indigenous history off the conceptual map'; Kauanui (2016, n. 7) adds Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973, Sayigh 1979 and Trask 1992/2000 before Wolfe.

strands.focus: Comparative collections and studies beyond the British settler dominions, including African settler and native political identities.

strands.title: The Indigenous reading: land, refusal, incommensurability
strands.focus: Indigenous political theory that takes up Wolfe's formula and redirects the field. Tuck and Yang: settler colonialism's violence 'is not temporally contained in the arrival of the settler but is reasserted each day of occupation. This is why Patrick Wolfe (1999) emphasizes that settler colonialism is a structure and not an event'; 'decolonization brings about the repatriation of Indigenous land and life; it is not a metaphor'; the settler–native–slave triad; 'settler moves to innocence'; 'an ethic of incommensurability' against reconciliation, which 'is about rescuing settler normalcy' (2012). Simpson: 'refusal' as 'an alternative to recognition politics in settler colonial society', consent 'as a technique of recognition and simultaneous dispossession' (2017, abstract; the 2014 book is known through its publisher page). Coulthard: settler colonialism 'territorially acquisitive in perpetuity'; in Canada the means of elimination changed but 'the ends have always remained the same: to shore up continued access to Indigenous peoples' territories' (2014, p. 125, as quoted by Englert); a 'place-based' reworking of primitive accumulation (publisher). Byrd and L. B. Simpson are unread and known only through catalogue metadata and other authors' citations; Moreton-Robinson is known through her publisher's checked description ('a white possession', 'the disavowal of Indigenous sovereignty'). These works have their own genealogies; in Canadian and US theses they are read with Wolfe (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23), and the user ruled (2026-10-12) that they may sit in more than one field.

strands.focus: Harris explains reserve-making as geographical dispossession, backed by state power, capital and settlers, and later reflects on the framework's boundaries. Carter's prairie reserve agriculture predates the paradigm.

strands.title: Gender, family and colonial nation-making
strands.focus: Gender, race, marriage and child removal in colonial British Columbia, the Prairie West, the American West and Australia. Perry is read in her 1995 and 2001/02 essays and in in-period reviews of On the Edge of Empire, the book itself unread; Carter (2008) and Jacobs (2009) remain at metadata level.

strands.focus: Settler self-examination after residential schools and in contemporary Canada; Regan's contents page names the 'peacemaker myth'. strands.title: Health, starvation and state policy
strands.focus: Daschuk's Plains history is the work most co-cited with Wolfe and Veracini by Canadian History PhDs: 19 of 58 citing theses in the 2026-10-12 pilot (Canadian strict History PhDs, 2009–26), and a 2020–25 entrant to the Canadian settler-colonial neighbourhood (support 12, lift 6.1) in the History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23. Its publisher describes 'a policy of starvation' that 'sparked widespread debate about genocide in Canada' and does not use 'settler colonialism'; the 2019 edition adds responses by Kelm, Mosby, Neylan and Woolford. His own framing remains unchecked; the TRC summary's 'cultural genocide' (2015) is the public text beside which the book is read. A comparison strand.
strands.works: James Daschuk, Clearing the Plains: Disease, Politics of Starvation, and the Loss of Aboriginal Life (Regina: University of Regina Press, 2013).

strands.title: Labour and the settler order
strands.focus: Integrates settler workers' ongoing appropriation of Indigenous land into Canadian working-class history.
strands.works: Fred Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework: Rethinking Canadian Working-Class History," Labour/Le Travail 83 (2019): 173–197.

strands.title: Critiques: fatalism, region, period, exploitation
strands.focus: From inside the theory, Macoun and Strakosch: SCT 'posits a structural inevitability', 'can depict colonization as structurally inevitable', risks 'colonial fatalism' and 'does not account for Indigenous lives'; yet 'the fact that settler colonialism struggles to narrate its own ending does not mean that it cannot end' (2013). Rowse: a 'teleology of elimination' (2014, abstract). Greer: one mode among several, dominant in some periods and regions (2019). Shoemaker: universal theory or English heritage? (2019). Englert: 'the elimination of the native … does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism'; settler colonies in Africa and South America 'were built on the exploitation of indigenous peoples'; accumulation by dispossession 'carried out by all classes of settlers, including by workers' (2020, with Kelley and Speed 2017).

William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 369–374.; Jeffrey Ostler and Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism in Early American History: Introduction," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 361–368.

strands.title: Indigenous studies and the field: who made it, whom it displaces
strands.focus: Kauanui: Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did', yet 'he tends to be most frequently cited as if he had'; 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; indigeneity is 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'; Warrior counted ASA panels and feared the field had become 'an answer to the chronic need for more attention to … Native and Indigenous studies' (2016). Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel: the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study' (2014). Goeman answers from the same field: Wolfe 'critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner' and his work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies' (2016). Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge the field (2019, abstract).
strands.works: Shino Konishi, "First Nations Scholars, Settler Colonial Studies, and Indigenous History," Australian Historical Studies 50, no. 3 (2019): 285–304.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).; Corey Snelgrove, Rita Kaur Dhamoon and Jeff Corntassel, "Unsettling Settler Colonialism: The Discourse and Politics of Settlers, and Solidarity with Indigenous Nations," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 2 (2014): 1–32.

strands.title: Slavery and Black studies critiques
strands.focus: How settler-colonial and decolonial frameworks place slavery and Black people. Wolfe 2006 (read) sets out the opposed racialisations of Black and Indigenous people in the United States; Tuck and Yang's settler–native–slave triad (read) is what Garba and Sorentino answer. Both authors' words are now read; the critics' remain at abstract level.
strands.works: Tapji Garba and Sara-Maria Sorentino, "Slavery Is a Metaphor: A Critical Commentary on Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's 'Decolonization Is Not a Metaphor'," Antipode 52, no. 3 (2020): 764–782.; Jared Sexton, "The Vel of Slavery: Tracking the Figure of the Unsovereign," Critical Sociology 42, nos. 4–5 (2016): 583–597.; Tiffany Lethabo King, The Black Shoals: Offshore Formations of Black and Native Studies (Durham: Duke University Press, 2019).

strands.title: Structure and its end: Wolfe and Veracini read together
strands.focus: Two emphases within one formula, not a documented exchange between opponents. Wolfe's structure is 'a continuity through time' that 'does not stop' with frontier homicide and 'has not been subject to election results' (2006). Veracini accepts the 'frequently quoted passage' and adds that 'the structure persistently pursues a specific end point' and 'extinguishes itself', so that settler colonialism 'covers its tracks' (2011): the end point is the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, which Veracini distinguishes from decolonisation. The History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) records the two authors co-cited by 3.0% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, a readership pairing that does not itself establish a dispute. Englert reads both as drawing 'a sharp analytical separation' between eliminatory settler and exploitative franchise colonies and finds the separation does not fit Africa or South America (2020); Macoun and Strakosch find in the structure a 'colonial fatalism' and recall the label 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world' (2013): these readings establish different emphases placed on the same structure. Veracini's obituary records Wolfe as 'still a Marxist' of 'the young Marx' for whom 'things are not things in themselves but relationships' (2016).
strands.works: Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native" (2006); Veracini, "Introducing settler colonial studies" (2011) and "Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016)" (2016); Macoun and Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory" (2013); Englert, "Settlers, Workers, and the Logic of Accumulation by Dispossession" (2020).

strands.title: Canadian history beside and under the frame, 2009–2020
strands.focus: Works that Canadian PhDs read with Wolfe and Veracini, few of which adopt his vocabulary. Treaty history (Miller 2009, a distinctive riser among Canadian PhDs inside the Indigenous family in the 2026-10-23 release), racialisation and law in British Columbia's 'contact zone' (Mawani 2009), settler self-examination after residential schools (Regan 2010; Battell Lowman and Barker 2015: 'Canada and Settler Colonialism', 'It's Always All About the Land'), starvation policy (Daschuk 2013), Indigenous women's work 'in modern Native ways' (McCallum 2014), the TRC's finding that Canada's policy aimed 'to eliminate Aboriginal governments … and … cause Aboriginal peoples to cease to exist as distinct … entities' and 'can best be described as "cultural genocide"' (2015), imperial family and archive (Perry 2015), women homesteaders in 'the spadework of British colonialism' who 'took part in dispossessing Indigenous people' (Carter 2016), the settler-colonial city (Hugill 2017), the settler order in working-class history (Burrill 2019), Japanese Canadian dispossession (Stanger-Ross 2020), and Harris's reflections (2020). Veracini's own history says the Canadian historiography was 'late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis' (2013). Publisher descriptions, not the books, are read; none of Miller, Daschuk, McCallum, Perry 2015, Carter 2016 or Stanger-Ross uses the phrase on its page.

(2017); Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework" (2019); Stanger-Ross, ed., Landscapes of Injustice (2020); Harris, A Bounded Land (2020).

strands.title: A field's institutions: journal, associations, memorials
strands.focus: NAISA founded 2008 after an ASA panel of 2002 asked whether American Studies could be 'an intellectual home' for Native studies (Kauanui). Settler Colonial Studies founded 2011 'in an open access format (entirely run on volunteer labour)' and moved to Taylor & Francis 'within two years' (Snelgrove et al.; Edmonds and Carey 2013). Wolfe edited paired issues of the journal and of AICRJ (2013) and answered the binary charge with The Settler Complex (2016). ASA 2015: Goldstein's reappraisal and Warrior's count of panels. Wolfe's death (18 February 2016) brought obituaries from the journal (Veracini), AICRJ (Goeman), Aboriginal History (Birch) and an American Quarterly forum (2017); a Festschrift followed (Race, Place, Trace, 2022).
strands.works: Kauanui (2016); Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014); Edmonds and Carey, "A New Beginning for Settler Colonial Studies" (2013); Wolfe, ed., "Recuperating Binarism" (2013) and The Settler Complex (2016); Veracini (2016); Goeman (2016); Birch (2016); American Quarterly 69:2 (2017); Slyomovics and Veracini, eds., Race, Place, Trace (2022).

ian_mckay.date_label: Tartanism Triumphant 1992 · The Quest of the Folk 1994 · 'A Note on Region' and the liberal order prospectus 2000 · later readings 2005, 2008, 2009
ian_mckay.description: Reads twentieth-century Nova Scotia's 'folk' as a cultural selection by folklorists, handicraft planners, writers and the tourist state, and as a local version of an international antimodernist wave (1992, 1994). In 2000 he proposed treating Canada as a project of liberal rule, to be studied through the implantation of liberalism across a heterogeneous terrain, and asked how 'region' fits that project. Later work turns to the Canadian left as a counter-project (2005, 2008) and answers the framework's critics (2009).

william_cronon.label: William Cronon
william_cronon.date_label: Changes in the Land 1983 · Nature's Metropolis 1991 · “The Trouble with Wilderness” 1995 · Environmental History forum 1996 · “The Riddle of the Apostle Islands” 2003 · AHA presidency 2012–13 · “Storytelling” 2013
william_cronon.description: A historian of North American environments who treats ecological change as a two-way relation between people and the rest of nature, worked out through property, markets and ideas of nature. Changes in the Land (1983) assumes that 'the interactions of the two are dialectical' and finds in colonial New England not a choice between landscapes with and without people but 'two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'. Nature’s Metropolis (1991) follows grain, lumber and meat between Chicago and its hinterland on the premise that 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together'. 'A Place for Stories' (1992) asks environmental historians for 'stories about stories about nature', and 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) calls wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'. Reviewers found the Chicago book distant from farmers and townspeople, or moralising; he replied that he saw 'no pure heroes or pure villains'. After 1995 the essay drew its own debate: Hays found in it 'a world of abstracted ideas' (1996, as quoted by Foreman), and Foreman told a wilderness-science conference that the 'Received Wilderness Idea' of 'Callicott, Cronon and other postmodern deconstructionist scholars' was 'a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground' (2000). Cronon answered in practice, asking that the Apostle Islands be managed 'as a historical wilderness', 'a storied wilderness' (2003). He edited the Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books (1994–2014) and, as 'the first self-described environmental historian ever to serve as president of the AHA', told the profession that 'Our core business is resurrection: helping the dead past live again' (2013).
william_cronon.representative_figures_and_works: William Cronon (b. 1954); Changes in the Land: Indians, Colonists, and the Ecology of New England (1983); “Modes of Prophecy and Production: Placing Nature in History” (JAH 1990); Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991); “Kennecott Journey: The Paths out of Town” (1992); “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (JAH 1992); “The Uses of Environmental History” (1993); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995). Readings: the Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response (1992); Sessions’s reply on wilderness (1996); his own afterword to Changes in the Land (2003). Later: 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (Orion, 2003); 'Storytelling' (AHR, 2013); Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books, series editor 1994–2014. Readers: Hays (1996, as quoted by Foreman); Callicott and Nelson, eds. (1998); Foreman (2000).
william_cronon.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-13: chapter 1 of Changes in the Land in an unpaginated web transcription; 'A Place for Stories' (JAH 1992; pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read) and 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author’s scan, journal pagination); 'Kennecott Journey' (1992); passages of 'The Trouble with Wilderness' in the author’s reflow; and the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response read in full. He places environmental history among the 'new' histories 'born or reenergized in the wake of the 1960s' (1993, p. 2), names Nash, Hays, Worster, Merchant, Tarr and Pyne as practitioners (pp. 2–3), footnotes lessons to Crosby, Richard White, McEvoy and others (pp. 8–10), and echoes Leopold (n. 11). bryan_d_palmer.label: Bryan D. Palmer
bryan_d_palmer.date_label: ‘Most Uncommon Common Men’ 1976 · A Culture in Conflict 1979 · ‘Response to Joan Scott’ 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions 1994 · ‘Radical Reasoning’ 2009
bryan_d_palmer.description: A Canadian historian of labour and the left who took up E. P. Thompson's account of class and culture and later defended historical materialism against the linguistic turn. His first essay in Labour/Le Travailleur (1976) traced artisan culture and restated what he called 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history': 'As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop'; the critic David Bercuson read his study of Hamilton's skilled workers (1979) as 'echoing E.P. Thompson' (1981). In the International Labor and Working-Class History forum of 1987 he answered Joan Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which on his reading reduced class and its material relations to discourse, while granting, as Ted McCoy (2021) quotes him, that 'to say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters'; and Descent into Discourse (1990) held, as the Marxist reviewer Alex Callinicos quoted it, that 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected', while granting that discourse theory 'contains insights and guides'. Scott replied that 'class struggle is produced in discourse', a discourse she took to include 'ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies', not words alone, and that there is no choice, 'as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender'; Callinicos, broadly sympathetic, suggested that his treatment of class might underestimate 'the objective determinants of subjective action' and noted that he took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. In 2009 he criticised Ian McKay's liberal order as, in his reading, 'a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework' that 'sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'.

Readings: Bercuson (1981); Scott’s reply (1987); Callinicos (1992); Dissenting Traditions (2021), with essays by Rogers, McCoy and Pearson.
