carl_berger.label: Carl Berger
carl_berger.date_label: The Sense of Power 1970 · The Writing of Canadian History 1976; 2nd ed. 1986
carl_berger.description: A University of Toronto historian of English-Canadian ideas. The Sense of Power (1970) is 'a study in Canadian nationalist thought': against the 'so-called liberal nationalist school', for which imperialism and nationalism added up to 'a struggle between the past and the future', he argued that 'Imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism', a 'type of awareness of nationality which rested upon a certain understanding of history, the national character, and the national mission'. The Writing of Canadian History (1976; second edition 1986) examines 'aspects of English-Canadian historical thought and literature since the turn of the century' through the 'central teachings' of Wrong, Shortt, Martin, Innis, Lower, Underhill, Creighton and Morton, and treats written history as 'a self-conscious effort to establish the meaning of experience for the present'; he left French-Canadian writing aside because the two language traditions had been 'preoccupied with the backgrounds of two rather different “nations”'. In period, Jacques Monet thought the imperialism thesis 'très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter' (1972), while Douglas Cole and Graham Carr held that it over-Canadianized a Britannic movement, Susan Mann Trofimenkoff called his imperialists' nationalism 'decidedly masculine' (1979), Allen Mills found that his account of all Canadian historians as nationalists put 'much too much weight on that over-used term' (1977), and Ronald Rudin rejected his assumption that historians were 'united by their search for the truth' (1997).
carl_berger.representative_figures_and_works: Carl Berger (b. 1939); ed., Imperialism and Nationalism, 1884–1914: A Conflict in Canadian Thought (1969); The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (1970; 2nd ed. 2013, with an introduction by Doug Owram); The Writing of Canadian History: Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900–1970 (1976; 2nd ed., … since 1900, 1986, with a new chapter, 'Tradition and the “New” History'); Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983). Readings: Monet (1972); Mills (1977); Terry Cook (1977–78); Trofimenkoff (1979); Carr (1982); Karr (1989); Rudin (1997). Later reading: Owram (2013).

Berger's own words are quoted from Google Books snippet views (The Sense of Power, 2013 printing with the 1970 pagination: introduction pp. 3, 9–10, conclusion p. 259; The Writing of Canadian History, 1986 edition: both prefaces and pp. 181, 261–262, 289, 298, 312), and are corroborated by in-period reviews read in full: Monet (1972), Mills (1977) and Terry Cook (1977–78). Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983) is checked at metadata level only. He is not presented as the originator of the imperialism thesis: Monet notes that Norman Penlington's Canada and Imperialism (1965) had already suggested it. Contested in period: Page, Cole and Nelles (1970, as Monet reports them), Cole (1971), Carr (1982, journal abstract), Karr (1989) on the elite group-biography method, Trofimenkoff (1979) on women, and Rudin (1997) on French-Canadian writing and on the assumption of a common search for truth. No in-period text found here faults The Writing of Canadian History for treating only male historians; Trofimenkoff's critique is of the field. Owram's 2013 introduction is a later reading.

ramsay_cook.label: Ramsay Cook
ramsay_cook.date_label: “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” 1967 · The Maple Leaf Forever 1971 · “Regionalism Unmasked” 1983 · The Regenerators 1985 · “Cabbages Not Kings” 1990 · “Identities Are Not Like Hats” 2000
ramsay_cook.description: An English-Canadian historian of nationalism, Quebec and Victorian thought. Attacking a nationalist manifesto in the centennial year, he suggested that 'instead of constantly deploring our lack of identity, we should attempt to understand and explain the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have. It might just be that it is in these limited identities that “Canadianism” is found' (1967, as quoted by Buckner); Careless made 'limited identities' a programme in 1969. Cook did not make region his unit of analysis: reviewing regional syntheses, he doubted 'the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions' and judged that 'as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (1983). The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social critics as replacing 'man's salvation' with 'a concern for social salvation', so that Christianity became 'less rather than more relevant' (as quoted by Gauvreau); Michael Gauvreau answered in 1991 that the book rests on 'military metaphors' that recent studies had abandoned, and a 1998 review named Cook, with David Marshall, the strongest advocate of the 'secularization thesis'. His lecture 'Cabbages Not Kings' (1990) proposed an ecological reading of contact in which 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world'. In the quarrel over national history he called the debate between 'nationalists' and 'limited identitarians' 'arid' (1993), and in 2000 he argued that identities are 'contingent' and 'multiple rather than single'.
ramsay_cook.representative_figures_and_works: Ramsay Cook (1931–2016); Canada and the French-Canadian Question (1966); “Canadian Centennial Cerebrations” (International Journal, 1967); The Maple Leaf Forever: Essays on Nationalism and Politics in Canada (1971); Canada 1896–1921: A Nation Transformed (1974, with Robert Craig Brown); “The Burden of Regionalism” (Acadiensis, 1977); “Regionalism Unmasked” (Acadiensis, 1983); The Regenerators: Social Criticism in Late Victorian English Canada (1985); “Cabbages Not Kings: Towards an Ecological Interpretation of Early Canadian History” (Journal of Canadian Studies, 1990–91); “The New History of Atlantic Canada” (Acadiensis, 1993); “‘Identities Are Not Like Hats’” (Canadian Historical Review, 2000). Readings: Careless (1969); Gaffield (1986); Karr (1989); Gauvreau (1991); Marshall (1993–94); Buckner (2000).

donald_creighton.label: Donald Creighton
donald_creighton.date_label: The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence 1937 · Dominion of the North 1944 · John A. Macdonald 1952, 1955 · CHA presidential address 1957 · “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” 1969 · Canada’s First Century 1970
donald_creighton.description: A Toronto historian whose The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) built Canadian history around the one river system 'that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent', which inspired Canadians 'to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior' (his own restatement of 1969); Dominion of the North (1944) calls the river 'the natural basis of a great commercial empire' and beaver fur 'the first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system'. His two-volume John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955) completed what he called 'a trilogy on one theme'; in 1969 he accepted 'the parentage of an idea' others called 'the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history', but rejected the story that his first book was 'the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis'. As president of the Canadian Historical Association (1957) he attacked the Liberal 'Authorized Version' of Canadian history and the imported 'Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'Frontier thesis', and in 1969 he traced the 'decline and fall' of the Empire of the St. Lawrence and of the Canada built on it, calling official bilingualism and a special position for Quebec 'a repudiation of the intentions of the Fathers of Confederation'. Contested in period: Michel Brunet (1953) found the Macdonald biography full of 'nombreux préjugés', Guy Frégault (1955) asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ?', and W. L. Morton, as Davis (1985) reports him, held that the metropolitan view he associated with Creighton seemed 'necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland'. From the late 1960s the national frame the Laurentian narrative supported gave way to regional history and 'limited identities' (Buckner, 2000).

Macdonald: The Young Politician (1952) and The Old Chieftain (1955); Presidential Address, Canadian Historical Association (1957); Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (1957); “The Decline and Fall of the Empire of the St. Lawrence” (1969); Canada’s First Century, 1867–1967 (1970). The 1957 and 1969 texts are polemics; their judgements of Mackenzie King, Quebec and bilingualism are recorded as his claims, not adopted. joy_parr.label: Joy Parr
joy_parr.date_label: Labouring Children 1980 · 'Nature and Hierarchy' 1985 · The Gender of Breadwinners 1990 · 'Gender History and Historical Practice' 1995 · Domestic Goods 1999 · Sensing Changes 2010
joy_parr.description: A Canadian historian of work, gender, childhood, consumption and the environment. In 1985 she wrote that what set women and children apart as historical subjects was not nature but 'proximity to power', and asked historians to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict'. The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) tested this in two Ontario towns, Paris, a knitting-mill town where most wage earners were women, and Hanover, a furniture town where most were men; reviewers quote it rejecting 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' and treating 'class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' as pairs whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. In the Left History exchange of 1995–96 Iacovetta and Kealey called her 'a major figure in the field' of gender history, while Sangster criticised the tie her 1995 essay drew between gender history and 'the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships'; the labour historian Craig Heron praised the book but found that it had 'suppressed the impact of class' in a 1949 strike. Labouring Children (1980) grew from her Yale thesis on British child immigrants; later books turned to postwar household goods (Domestic Goods, 1999) and to sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change (Sensing Changes, 2010).
joy_parr.representative_figures_and_works: Joy Parr (1949–2024); PhD Yale 1977 ('The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924'); Labouring Children: British Immigrant Apprentices to Canada, 1869–1924 (1980); Childhood and Family in Canadian History (ed., 1982); “Nature and Hierarchy: Reflections on Writing the History of Women and Children” (Atlantis, 1985); “Disaggregating the Sexual Division of Labour” (CSSH, 1988); The Gender of Breadwinners: Women, Men, and Change in Two Industrial Towns, 1880–1950 (1990); “Gender History and Historical Practice” (CHR, 1995; reprinted in Gender and History in Canada, ed. with Mark Rosenfeld, 1996); “Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada” (ILWCH, 1999); Domestic Goods: The Material, the Moral, and the Economic in the Postwar Years (1999). After 2000: “Smells Like?” (Environmental History, 2006); Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (2010). Readings: Drystek (1980); Heron, Guildford, Scheinberg and Dennis (1991); Bertaux (1992); Benson (1993); the Left History exchange (Sangster 1995, 1996; Dubinsky and Marks 1996; Iacovetta and Kealey 1996); Brush (2000); Owram (2001); Jackson and Rumiel (2011).

ranajit_guha.label: Ranajit Guha
ranajit_guha.date_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal 1963 · “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” 1982 · Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency 1983 · “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency” 1983 · “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography” 1989 (book 1997) · History at the Limit of World-History 2002
ranajit_guha.description: A historian of colonial India, who taught at Sussex and the Australian National University and edited Subaltern Studies from its first volume (1982) until he left the editorial team in 1988. The opening statement holds that the historiography of Indian nationalism 'has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism', and that it leaves out 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain' that 'neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', while allowing 'a great deal of overlap' between the two (1982). Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) attributes 'a consciousness' to the rebel peasant, holds that Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India', and reads that consciousness through the records of counter-insurgency; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) finds colonial, nationalist and radical histories alike making the rebel 'only a contingent element in another history with another subject'. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989; book 1997) defines hegemony, against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony', as dominance in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', and argues that colonial dominance had 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony'. In period, Spivak (1985) read the recovery of subaltern consciousness as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', O'Hanlon (1988) found 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself', Bayly (1988) found that the approach sometimes seemed to postulate an 'unchanging peasantry', and Sarkar (1997) an 'unnoticed drift' towards nationalist positions 'even in Guha's initial formulation of the project'. His first book, A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963), traced the Permanent Settlement to the mercantilist, physiocratic and classical political economy of East India Company officials, in Gurminder Bhambra’s reading (2024), which faults it for leaving the colonial context aside. Reviewing Dominance without Hegemony, Amalendu Chakraborty (2000) found the subalterns’ own voices missing from what he called “a mere armchair ideological ‘discourse’”. After 2000, History at the Limit of World-History (2002), lectures given at Columbia’s Italian Academy, takes Hegel’s World-history to task as a statist frame and asks historians to learn from literature the “historicality” of everyday life, in its reviewers’ accounts; Guha’s claim, as Bernardo Michael quotes it, is that World-History reached India “as an instrument of the East India Company’s colonial project”. Michael welcomed the turn to everyday life but warned that “losing sight of the state ... might mean the loss of it as an object of critique”; he also found the argument “mostly confined to the conceptual level”, without showing how Hegel’s ideas became colonial practice (2004). Dipesh Chakrabarty later called the book “his farewell to the discipline of history”, after which Guha wrote in Bengali (2024). Vivek Chibber’s Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital (2013) made Dominance without Hegemony a central target, arguing that its contrast between Indian and European bourgeoisies rests on “a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions”; William Sewell agreed that Guha’s portrayal of the English and French revolutions was “standard-issue orthodox Marxism”, while Partha Chatterjee, as Chibber reports him, denied that Guha made claims about those revolutions at all (2013–14).

After 2000: History at the Limit of World-History (Columbia University Press, 2002). Readings: Spivak (1985); O'Hanlon (1988); Bayly (1988); Sarkar (1997); Chakraborty (2000); Chakrabarty (2000); Michael (2004); Chibber (2013–14) and the Journal of World-Systems Research symposium, with Sewell, Steinmetz and Cumings (2014); Holmwood, Bhambra and Seth (2024); Chakrabarty (2024).

gregory_s_kealey.label: Gregory S. Kealey
gregory_s_kealey.date_label: ‘The Honest Workingman’ 1976 · ‘The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing’ 1978 · Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism 1980 · ‘Prospects in the 1980s’ 1981 · Dreaming of What Might Be (with Palmer) 1982 · ‘1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt’ 1984 · Class, Gender, and Region 1988 · RCMP Security Bulletins (with Whitaker) 1989–97 · Spying on Canadians 2017
gregory_s_kealey.description: A Canadian historian of the working class, and later of political policing, who argued for putting class at the centre of Canadian history. Of Toronto's craftsmen he wrote that 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized', amounting to 'a high degree of workers' control of production' (1976); in 1981 he held that 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history', and he criticised the regional turn, under which 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere', as he had criticised the 'so-called "limited identities"' in 1978. David Brody, reviewing Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980), found it marked by 'what might be termed the Gutman school' and a useful foundation, but judged that Kealey had 'overreached himself' in its interpretation; Bettina Bradbury (1987) faulted him and Bryan Palmer for partially dismissing a Knights of Labor editor's picture of the ideal working-class wife as 'crude moralizing', and Joan Sangster (2000) found in both men's early books 'a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere'. From the late 1980s he edited the RCMP's security bulletins with Reg Whitaker and studied state surveillance of labour and the left, concluding that 'For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946' (1992).

jennifer_s_h_brown.label: Jennifer S. H. Brown
jennifer_s_h_brown.date_label: Strangers in Blood 1980 · “Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities” 1983 · The New Peoples (ed. with Peterson) 1985 · The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman) 1988 · “Ethnohistorians: Strange Bedfellows, Kindred Spirits” 1991 · Reading Beyond Words (ed. with Vibert) 1996 · An Ethnohistorian in Rupert’s Land 2017
jennifer_s_h_brown.description: An anthropologist and historian of fur-trade families, the Métis, and Cree and Ojibwe history in the old Hudson's Bay Company territory. Strangers in Blood (1980) compared Hudson's Bay Company officers and North West Company partners as husbands and fathers; as a 1981 reviewer quoted it, the title took the British legal term for any relationship 'that the law refused to admit as legitimate' as 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians' in the fur trade. In 1983 she asked how women shaped Métis emergence, finding among North West Company fathers who had children baptized in Montreal that daughters were twice as likely as sons to stay in the Indian country, and in 1985 she co-edited with Jacqueline Peterson The New Peoples: Being and Becoming Métis in North America. As president of the American Society for Ethnohistory she spoke of 'our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory' (1991). A 1981 reviewer found the book weighed down by 'bits of anthropological theory'; Emma LaRocque (1999) placed her with Van Kirk in a 'neo cross-cultural approach', 'a much improved approach' on earlier work that still othered its subjects; and later scholarship rejects defining Métis by mixed descent, the biological starting point ('the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups') that her 1983 essay set against a complex social history.

bruce_curtis.label: Bruce Curtis
bruce_curtis.date_label: With Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation” 1985 · Building the Educational State 1988 · True Government by Choice Men? 1992 · The Politics of Population 2001 · “After ‘Canada’” 2009 · Ruling by Schooling Quebec 2012
bruce_curtis.description: A historical sociologist (Carleton University) whose studies of schooling, school inspection and the census in the Canadas read administration as a means of rule. In Building the Educational State (1988), as a reviewer quotes it, education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (p. 110), and the educational state was built 'only through the destruction of a prior educational organization' (p. 15); in True Government by Choice Men? (1992) 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (p. 32). His census history (2001) holds that 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (p. 305, as Belshaw quotes it), and in a 1996 review he wrote that 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns'. Reviewers credited his joining of Foucault's analysis of power to a Marxist theory of state formation but found gender relations missing (Davey 1989; Miller 1993), and Bryan Palmer judged the inspection study, taken as a model, 'overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (1993). In the debate over Ian McKay's liberal order framework, Nancy Christie cites 'Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality' (2009).
bruce_curtis.representative_figures_and_works: Bruce Curtis (b. 1950); with Philip Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation: A Preliminary Statement” (CHA Historical Papers, 1985); Building the Educational State: Canada West, 1836–1871 (1988); True Government by Choice Men? bruce_curtis.scope_note: This entry presents Curtis's state-formation studies of schooling, inspection and the census (1985–2001) and their place in the liberal order debate. The 1985 article with Corrigan, the 2009 chapter and Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012) are title- or summary-level only. He is a sociologist, not a historian by department; the atlas's moral regulation entry treats his state-formation work as shared ground with the liberal order framework, not membership.

allan_greer.label: Allan Greer
allan_greer.date_label: “Fur-Trade Labour” 1981 · “A Critique of Pentland” and Peasant, Lord, and Merchant 1985 · Colonial Leviathan (ed. with Radforth) 1992 · The Patriots and the People 1993 · Property and Dispossession 2018 · “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” 2019
allan_greer.description: A historian of Lower Canada and colonial North America whose rural social history described a feudal, household-centred habitant society: in 1985 he held that Lower Canadian 'agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production', with part of the surplus 'diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions', a view he set against both Ouellet's routine-bound peasant (1981) and the commercial farmer of Paquet and Wallot, while allowing that 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' (1985). The same essay, a critique of Clare Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, faulted the staples tradition of Innis and Creighton for confining attention to 'relations of exchange'. With Ian Radforth he edited Colonial Leviathan (1992), on mid-nineteenth-century state formation, which Bryan Palmer found to lack coherence (1993) and which Greer later said 'neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (2019); his history of the 1837 rebellion (1993) is known here through reviewers, who read it as breaking with Ouellet's manipulated peasantry. His later work on 'property formation' (2018) and his 2019 lecture treat settler colonialism as one mode of colonial invasion among several, 'a dominant force in some periods and regions' that 'fades to insignificance in others', while insisting 'I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory'.

cole_harris.label: Cole Harris
cole_harris.date_label: The Seigneurial System in Early Canada 1966 · Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (editor) 1987 · The Resettlement of British Columbia 1997 · ‘Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia’ 1997–98 · Making Native Space 2002 · ‘Revisiting the Native Land Question’ 2003 · ‘How Did Colonialism Dispossess?’ 2004 · A Bounded Land 2020
cole_harris.description: A Canadian historical geographer of early Canada and of colonialism in British Columbia. He edited the first volume of the Historical Atlas of Canada (1987), whose preface says it sought 'to emphasize the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life rather than the more usual fare of historical atlases' (as quoted by MacDonald, 1990). From the 1990s he wrote British Columbia's colonization as geographical change. Against the 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era history he set 'epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (1997–98). He explained the reserve system as dispossession: its capacity 'rested on raw firepower', its momentum 'came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods', and its legitimation 'lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery' (2003); in 2004 he argued that the emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'. Reviewers found few Native voices in the work: Tina Loo (1998) saw Native peoples 'emerge as victims' in The Resettlement of British Columbia, and Val Napoleon (2004) wrote that Making Native Space 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history' and that Harris 'should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices' where history gave way to proposals for the future.

capitalismdebates.label: Capitalism, divergence and industrialisation
capitalismdebates.date_label: Capitalism and Slavery 1944 · Dobb–Sweezy 1950 · Brenner debate 1976–85 · Wrigley 1988 · de Vries 1994 · The Great Divergence 2000 · Allen and The Enlightened Economy 2009 · Empire of Cotton 2014 · Hilt 2017 · Burnard and Riello 2020
capitalismdebates.description: A set of linked arguments about why capitalism, industrialisation and Western wealth arose where and when they did. Marxist historians disputed whether trade or class relations ended feudalism: Dobb answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950). Brenner's property-relations thesis (1976) opened a second round, in which Bois called his approach 'political Marxism' and Wood made it a programme. Economic historians slowed the British Industrial Revolution while reasserting 'an important discontinuity' (Crafts and Harley, 1992), and Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' it; explanations multiplied in Wrigley's escape from an 'organic economy', de Vries's 'industrious revolution', Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' and Allen's high wages and cheap energy. Wong challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm; Pomeranz acknowledged that method while giving greater weight to global conjunctures, ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; critics answered from property relations, knowledge, wages and the state. Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) returned through Inikori, the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and an American 'history of capitalism' whose economic-historian critics charged 'specious arguments' (Hilt, 2017). Readers join these debates themselves: Burnard and Riello set the new history of capitalism beside the Brenner debate and Pomeranz (2020).

strands.title: The transition debate: Dobb, Sweezy and their readers, 1946–1976
strands.focus: Dobb's Studies (1946) defined feudalism by the coercive relation between producer and lord; Sweezy (1950) answered that feudalism was 'a system of production for use' dissolved by 'causes external to the system', above all trade, while granting that 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Dobb replied that trade 'exercised its influence to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts', and carried the argument to the absolutist state and the English Revolution. Takahashi (1952) developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour, and pressed for fuller French and German comparison. Hilton collected the exchange with later essays in 1976. Positions within one Marxist debate, not a school. The field strands marx/transition and economic/marxist keep each author's own contribution.

strands.title: Against 'neo-Smithian Marxism': Brenner on Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein, 1977
strands.focus: Brenner traced Wallerstein's world-system and Frank's development of underdevelopment back to Sweezy's side of the 1950 debate and, through it, to 'the model put forward by Adam Smith'. He acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb, and credited Frank with breaking 'the suffocating orthodoxies' of stage theory. Callinicos (1990) called the critique 'a valuable corrective'. See dependency/worldsystems for Wallerstein's own account.
strands.works: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977); Wallerstein, The Modern World-System I (1974); Frank (1966–)

strands.title: The Brenner debate in Past and Present, 1976–1985
strands.focus: Brenner argued that class structure decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth. Postan and Hatcher called his charges against them 'groundless'; Le Roy Ladurie defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model; Croot and Parker, Wunder and Klíma tested his English, French, German and Bohemian comparisons; Bois agreed against 'the Malthusian model' but not with Brenner's method. Brenner's reply (1982) spoke of 'social-property systems'. Hilton introduced the collection (1985) as 'a continuation' of the transition debate. The respondents are read only in their Cambridge Core openings; their later pages are unread, and Bois's specified later passages (pp. 115–116) are known only as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990); see annales/serial for Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc.
strands.works: Past and Present 70 (1976) to 97 (1982); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985)

strands.title: Political Marxism: from Bois's charge to a school, 1978–2016
strands.focus: Bois called Brenner's approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (1978, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). By the accounts of Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), Wood accepted the label while rejecting the charge of voluntarism. She argued that 'the economic' and 'the political' are differently joined in pre-capitalist and capitalist societies (1981), against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism. Critics answered that it was 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos) and that Brenner, taking up Dobb, narrowed class struggle to the countryside (Harman).
strands.works: Bois (1978); Wood, 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (NLR, 1981), Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); Harman (1989); Callinicos, 'The Limits of "Political Marxism"' (NLR, 1990); Harman and Brenner (2004, printed 2006); Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016) on Wood

strands.title: The origin of capitalism and its critics, 1991–2004
strands.focus: Wood argued that England was 'the world's first capitalist society' (1991), siding with Thompson against the Nairn–Anderson theses. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she set the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' against the 'commercialization model'; The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), unread here, is known through its jacket and McAuley's quotations. McAuley (2001), drawing on Blaut, criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal; Wood replied that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. This exchange joins the strand to the slavery and divergence components.
strands.works: Wood, The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), replies (2002); McAuley (2001)

strands.title: Revolution or gradual growth? The Industrial Revolution revised, 1884–1994
strands.focus: Toynbee's posthumous lectures (1884) defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations'. Crafts and Harley's output estimates slowed its pace while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992); Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' the subject and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992). De Vries (1994) read the revisionists as 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off"', not pulling down the pillars.
strands.works: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (1884); Crafts and Harley (1992); Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper; EHR 1992); de Vries (JEH 1994), pp. 249–251; see historicalecon/british_teaching

strands.title: Rural industry and industrious households, 1972–2016
strands.focus: Mendels (1972) treated market-oriented rural industry as 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper', and later called it 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); the Göttingen group (Kriedte, Medick, Schlumbohm, 1977) placed rural industry in 'the genesis of capitalism'. Coleman (1983) titled his critique 'a concept too many'. De Vries's 'industrious revolution' (1994; 2008), a term he and van Nederveen Meerkerk trace to Akira Hayami, made household labour and demand precede the Industrial Revolution; reviewers asked whether consumption had become 'a new deus ex machina' (2009). Rosenband (2016), from French and English papermaking, challenged the model: paperworkers 'already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness', and women and adolescents worked for wages long before it (abstract). See economic/household_demand, consumption/household_labor and global/protoindustry_trade_limits for the field contributions.
strands.works: Mendels (JEH 1972) and NYRB letter (1984); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977; English 1981); Medick (1976); Coleman (1983); de Vries (1994; 2008); van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Rosenband (2016)

strands.title: Why Britain? Energy, knowledge and wages, 1988–2023
strands.focus: Wrigley (1988) questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime. Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' was 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley questioned whether the Industrial Enlightenment explained economic change or largely redescribed it (2010). Allen (2009) argued that 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap', so 'it paid to invent it there'; Humphries charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' (2013), and Allen replied with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract). Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda found that, across English counties, industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023); the result concerns differences within England, not Britain's international wage advantage. The article sets it 'directly counter' to Allen's argument (pp. 60–61), as their 2014 essay had argued from British workers' human capital against his high wages. Clark and Jacks's coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England's possession of coal reserves (2007). See economic/wrigley_growth and technology/invention_adoption.
strands.works: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), The Path to Sustained Growth (2016); Mokyr (2002 paper), The Enlightened Economy (2009); Harley (2010); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Clark and Jacks (2007)

strands.title: The Great Divergence and the so-called California School, 1997–2021
strands.focus: Wong (1997) challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm. Pomeranz (2000) followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed' while giving 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures', and greater weight to ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; he dated divergence late. Readers attribute the label 'California School' to Goldstone (Frank 2001; Vries 2009), whose 'efflorescences' (2002) put pre-modern growth outside Europe too while locating the modern breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture. Frank's ReOrient (1998) and a debate with Landes scheduled for December 1998, announced in a notice written from Frank's side, marked the polemical poles. Parthasarathi carried the argument to India (2011). Rosenthal and Wong explained divergence by political fragmentation and war (2011, as Ma's review reports and Wong restated in 2016); Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence'. Critics answered from property relations (Brenner and Isett 2002), knowledge (Mokyr 2002, 2012), wages and national accounts (Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen et al. 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) and the state (Vries 2009, 2013). The Huang–Pomeranz exchange stays in economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute.

(2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021); see global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources

strands.title: Capitalism and Slavery and its critics: the Williams thesis, 1944–2020
strands.focus: Williams (1944) advanced distinct propositions, which readers keep apart: that slave-trade and plantation wealth financed and stimulated British industry; that slave-derived wealth mattered in eighteenth-century Britain; and that the West Indies' economic decline, with changing economic interests, explains abolition. Drescher's Econocide (1977), in its publisher's description, challenged decline-based explanations of the 1807 abolition and stressed public mobilisation; Solow and Engerman's volume (1987) sifted the 'legacy'. Solow judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello), while Eltis and Engerman (2000), as Hilt and Burnard and Riello report them, judged its growth linkages to British industry small. Inikori (2002), as O'Rourke reports, reasserted the thesis through Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers. Hall (2014) and Burnard and Riello (2020) identify modified Williams arguments in Pomeranz and Inikori. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership team investigates slave-ownership's British legacies; its compensation evidence supports some Williams propositions, on slave-derived wealth, and qualifies the decline thesis, while leaving the industrialisation controversy unresolved ('Our material cannot resolve these controversies'). See economic/empire and atlantic/earlier.
strands.works: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Drescher, Econocide (1977) and 'Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years' (1997); Solow and Engerman (eds), British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000); Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002); Hall et al., Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014)

strands.title: Slavery's capitalism and its economic-historian critics, 2013–2020
strands.focus: This strand selects the slavery controversy within the broader history of capitalism, a field whose early definition by Beckert, Hilt notes, is so broad that it 'includes most of the fields of labor, political, social, and business history', and whose work, Regele notes, began before the 2007–2009 financial crisis. Mainly Americanist historians, publicised as historians of capitalism in 2013, put slavery at the centre of American and global capitalism: Johnson's River of Dark Dreams (2013; Johnson does not count himself a historian of capitalism, Hilt notes), Baptist's argument, in Hilt's account, that torture drove cotton productivity (2014), Beckert's 'war capitalism' (2014) and Beckert and Rockman's Slavery's Capitalism (2016). Olmstead and Rhode answered that the books 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017); Hilt, that 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine' them as social criticism, while granting that economic research supports some of their arguments and calling for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (2017); Burnard and Riello, that US cotton came 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution' (2020). Readers trace the movement to Polanyi, the 2008 crisis and a turn from labour history (Hilt; Regele) and to Williams and Pomeranz (Burnard and Riello). Fogel and Engerman's earlier slavery debate stays in quant/slavery_debate.
strands.works: Johnson, River of Dark Dreams (2013); Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told (2014); Beckert, Empire of Cotton (2014); Beckert and Rockman (eds), Slavery’s Capitalism (2016); Olmstead and Rhode (AHA 2017; EEH 2018); Hilt (JEH 2017); Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020); Regele (2023)

strands.title: Corporate capitalism, finance and public power
strands.focus: White’s Railroaded asks how debt-financed corporations, public subsidies and political markets could enrich insiders despite repeated corporate failure. This is an inquiry into the institutional operation of American capitalism, distinct from the feudal transition, industrial growth and slavery controversies grouped elsewhere here.

ann_laura_stoler.label: Ann Laura Stoler
ann_laura_stoler.date_label: 'Tensions of Empire' (with Cooper) 1989 · Race and the Education of Desire 1995 · Tensions of Empire 1997 · 'Tense and Tender Ties' 2001 · 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' 2002 · Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power 2002 · Haunted by Empire 2006 · Along the Archival Grain 2009 · Imperial Debris 2013 · Duress 2016
ann_laura_stoler.description: An American anthropologist of Dutch and French colonial rule who moved from Sumatra's plantation belt to the colonial archive itself. With Frederick Cooper she set an agenda for reading metropole and colony together (1989; 1997). Race and the Education of Desire (1995) questioned race and empire in Foucault's history of sexuality; Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002) asked why 'Foucault's elusive and suggestive treatment of race still remains so marginal to what colonial historians take from him' (p. 141) and treated 'colonizer/colonized' as 'a historically shifting pair of social categories that needs to be explained' (p. 13; both as quoted by Ottevaere, 2004). 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002) asked scholars to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject'; Along the Archival Grain (2009) read Dutch records 'along the grain' for 'the pulse of the archive' (p. 35, as quoted by Schulte Nordholt) and 'the habits of the colonial heart' (p. 53, as quoted by Gouda). Imperial Debris (2013) and Duress (2016) turned to ruination and 'imperial durabilities'. Gouda: in postcolonial studies 'paying homage to Ann Stoler's work has become de rigueur' (2009).
ann_laura_stoler.representative_figures_and_works: Ann Laura Stoler (b. 1949); Capitalism and Confrontation in Sumatra's Plantation Belt, 1870–1979 (1985); with Frederick Cooper, 'Tensions of Empire' (American Ethnologist, 1989) and Tensions of Empire (eds, 1997); Race and the Education of Desire (1995); 'Tense and Tender Ties' (JAH, 2001); 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (Archival Science, 2002); Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002; 2nd ed. 2010); ed., Haunted by Empire (2006); with McGranahan and Perdue, eds, Imperial Formations (2007); Along the Archival Grain (2009); ed., Imperial Debris (2013); Duress (2016); Interior Frontiers (2022). Readers: Dawn Ottevaere (2004); Frances Gouda, Remco Raben, Henk Schulte Nordholt (2009); Ronald Schultz (2015).
ann_laura_stoler.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md §§1–2, 6): the abstract and reference list of the 2002 Archival Science essay; the contents of Along the Archival Grain and three reviews from the Bijdragen debate (Gouda and Schulte Nordholt in full, Raben's first page) with the first paragraph of Stoler's reply; Ottevaere's H-Net review of Carnal Knowledge (in full) and the UC Press contents; Schultz's H-Net review of Imperial Debris (in full); the Duke pages for Haunted by Empire and Duress. Her 2002 notes cite Trouillot's Silencing the Past three times; no sentence of hers on Trouillot was read. Quotations from the 2009 book are 'as quoted by' Gouda or Schulte Nordholt, from Carnal Knowledge 'as quoted by' Ottevaere, from Imperial Debris 'as quoted by' Schultz, with their page numbers.
